Pacific slopehead parrotfish, Chlorurus frontalis, attains an ultimate total length of 50 centimeters [Li = 50 centimeters], a size that distinguishes it among the larger members of the parrotfish assemblage on Pacific coral reefs. Juveniles settle from the plankton at an exceedingly small size, with the estimated wet weight at birth being just 0.00023 grams [Wwb = 0.00023 grams], a value consistent with the tiny pelagic eggs typical of labrid fishes. This minute initial mass belies the substantial growth trajectory required to reach the maximum adult body mass of 2100 grams [Wwi = 2100 grams], which individuals achieve through sustained grazing on epilithic algal turfs and endolithic microborers. The transformation from a 0.00023 gram post-larval recruit to a 2100 gram terminal phase male requires a roughly nine-million-fold increase in tissue mass, highlighting the species’ considerable capacity for somatic expansion over its lifespan.

The onset of reproductive capability is tied to body size rather than strictly to age, with puberty occurring when individuals reach a total length of 30 centimeters [Lp = 30 centimeters]. At this length, a female typically has a wet weight of approximately 431 grams [Wwp = approximately 431 grams], reflecting the allometric relationship between length and mass derived from field specimens. The ecological significance of this size threshold is linked to the species’ social structure: smaller individuals generally function as initial-phase females, and only upon reaching a larger body size do some undergo protogynous sex change to become terminal-phase males that defend spawning territories. This size-based mating system means that the 30 centimeter mark represents not merely the onset of gametogenesis but also the size at which individuals can actively participate in the seasonal reproductive aggregations. The length at puberty thus defines the demographic window for first spawning within the population.

The gonadosomatic index (GSI) was estimated at approximately 12% [GSI = approximately 12%] at a water temperature of 27.5 °C [T = 27.5 °C]. The species is thought to participate in multiple spawning events annually, with a presumed frequency of three spawnings per year, which aligns with the protracted breeding seasons observed across much of its geographic range.

Longevity in Chlorurus frontalis has been estimated from otolith increment analysis and growth modeling, with the maximum recorded lifespan reaching approximately 4745 days [am = approximately 4745 days] under the prevailing thermal regime of 27.5 °C [T = 27.5 °C]. This extended lifespan, equating to roughly thirteen years, positions the Pacific slopehead parrotfish as a relatively long-lived member of the parrotfish guild, consistent with its large ultimate body size and iteroparous reproductive strategy. Individuals that persist for over a decade have the opportunity to undergo the full sequence of color and sex changes characteristic of the species, from initial-phase female to terminal-phase male. The slow pace of senescence in this species may be linked to its grazing diet, which involves constant but low-intensity foraging activity, as well as the availability of shelter-rich reef habitats that reduce predation risk for larger adults.

Age-related mortality increases notably after the species has passed its prime reproductive years, and the oldest documented individuals are invariably large terminal-phase males that have dominated spawning sites for multiple seasons. The combination of reaching a total length of 50 centimeters [Li = 50 centimeters] and attaining an adult mass of 2100 grams [Wwi = 2100 grams] represents the pinnacle of somatic growth for this species, and such individuals are rarely observed beyond the maximum age threshold. The physiological demands of maintaining a body mass of 2100 grams over a lifespan of nearly 4745 days involve substantial energetic costs, particularly for territory defense and gamete production during the breeding season. Comparative data from other scarine labrids suggest that this longevity is facilitated by the species’ ability to exploit a stable food resource, namely the carbonate matrix of dead coral substrates, which supports consistent year-round feeding.
